zz-eoline.theory: La EOLine es el paso definitorio del ZZ. Cuenta las aristas mal orientadas (aristas que no pueden resolverse solo con R, L, U, D). Un número par de aristas mal orientadas es orientable. Coloca DF y DB mientras corriges las mal orientadas. Tras la EOLine, el cubo se resuelve usando solo movimientos R, U y L.
drills: Practica contar aristas mal orientadas — identifica todas en menos de 5 segundos
Planifica la EOLine en la inspección — objetivo: 8-10 movimientos

zz-eocross.title: EOCross
zz-eocross.subtitle: Orienta las aristas mientras resuelves la cruz completa (no solo la línea) para un mejor F2L
zz-eocross.description: Transición de EOLine a EOCross: orienta todas las aristas Y resuelve la cruz completa (aristas DF, DB, DL, DR) en un paso para un mejor lookahead.
zz-eocross.theory: La EOCross usa más movimientos que la EOLine pero prepara una fase F2L mucho mejor. Con la cruz completa resuelta y todas las aristas orientadas, el F2L queda sin rotaciones por definición. La mayoría de los cuberos ZZ modernos prefieren la EOCross por sus ventajas ergonómicas.
drills: Planifica la EOCross en la inspección — objetivo: 12-14 movimientos
Compara resoluciones con EOLine vs EOCross para encontrar tu preferencia

zz-f2l.title: F2L de ZZ
zz-f2l.subtitle: F2L sin rotaciones usando solo R, U y L con todas las aristas orientadas
zz-f2l.description: Resuelve pares F2L usando solo movimientos R, U y L — sin rotaciones del cubo porque todas las aristas están pre-orientadas. Céntrate en la eficiencia de construcción de bloques.
zz-f2l.theory: La principal ventaja del F2L de ZZ: CERO rotaciones. Todos los pares se resuelven en el hemisferio frontal de 180°. Los pares pueden ir a las ranuras RF, LF, RB o LB con la misma facilidad. Esto entrena habilidades de resolución sin rotaciones que se transfieren directamente al CFOP.
drills: Practica solo el F2L de ZZ (detente tras el F2L) — objetivo: sub-8s
Compara el número de movimientos con tu F2L de CFOP para ver las ganancias de eficiencia

zz-coll-epll.title: COLL+EPLL de ZZ
zz-coll-epll.subtitle: Usa COLL para el control de esquinas y EPLL para la permutación rápida de aristas
zz-coll-epll.description: Aplica COLL (40 casos) para resolver las esquinas tras el F2L y usa luego EPLL (4 casos: Ua, Ub, H, Z) para terminar — la última capa ZZ experta estándar.
zz-coll-epll.theory: Como el ZZ orienta todas las aristas en el primer paso, la cruz de la última capa está siempre formada tras el F2L. Esto convierte al COLL en la elección natural: resuelve las esquinas en un paso, dejando solo los 4 PLL de aristas rápidos. Es más eficiente que el OLL+PLL estándar.
drills: Combina el reconocimiento COLL con la ejecución EPLL en un único flujo
Objetivo: COLL+EPLL en menos de 3,5s en total

zz-zbll.title: De ZZ a ZBLL
zz-zbll.subtitle: Integración completa del ZBLL — la última capa ZZ definitiva porque las aristas siempre están orientadas
zz-zbll.description: Aprovecha la orientación garantizada de aristas del ZZ para usar ZBLL en una última capa de un vistazo — resolviendo OLL y PLL simultáneamente en cada resolución.
zz-zbll.theory: ZZ + ZBLL es un emparejamiento natural: el ZZ garantiza aristas LL orientadas, que es exactamente el prerrequisito del ZBLL. Esto significa que CADA resolución termina con una última capa de un vistazo. Combinado con el F2L sin rotaciones, es uno de los sistemas de resolución más eficientes posibles.
drills: Solo casos ZBLL aplicables (aristas ya orientadas — el set completo es utilizable)
Practica ZZ específicamente con ZBLL para los subconjuntos T y U primero

zz-ct.title: ZZ-CT
zz-ct.subtitle: ZZ con Corner Twisty — inserta el último par resolviendo la CP para terminar con 2GLL
zz-ct.description: Aplica la variante ZZ-CT: usa TSLE (última arista estilo tran) durante la inserción del par final y luego 2GLL para una última capa 2-gen.
zz-ct.theory: El ZZ-CT es una alternativa al ZBLL. El TSLE inserta la última arista F2L mientras orienta las esquinas (~100 casos). Luego el 2GLL resuelve el resto usando solo movimientos R y U. Cambia el número de algoritmos del ZBLL por un sistema de 2 pasos con mejor ergonomía.
drills: Aprende el TSLE para las posiciones más comunes de la última arista de la ranura
Practica el reconocimiento 2GLL (variantes de PLL 2-gen y ZBLL)

zz-full-mastery.title: Dominio completo de ZZ
zz-full-mastery.subtitle: Soltura total de ZZ con capacidad sub-10 lista para competición
zz-full-mastery.description: Logra el dominio completo del ZZ: EOCross eficiente, F2L sin rotaciones optimizado y última capa rápida con ZBLL o CT — capaz de resoluciones sub-8.
zz-full-mastery.theory: El ZZ a nivel de élite combina lo mejor de todos los mundos: resolución sin rotaciones, última capa de un vistazo y bajo número de movimientos. Menos cuberos punteros usan ZZ que CFOP, pero quienes lo dominan logran una eficiencia notable. Número medio de movimientos: 45-50.
drills: Completa 1000 resoluciones de ZZ registrando la eficiencia de la EOCross y la velocidad de la última capa
Objetivo: EOCross en ≤12 movimientos, F2L sub-6s, última capa sub-2s

bld-old-pochmann.title: Old Pochmann Method
bld-old-pochmann.subtitle: Solve edges and corners one piece at a time using the classic BLD method
bld-old-pochmann.description: Learn the Old Pochmann method: use a fixed buffer piece and swap individual edges/corners using T-Perm and Y-Perm — the entry point to blindfolded solving.
bld-old-pochmann.theory: OP uses a buffer piece (UR for edges, UBR for corners) and swaps it with the target piece using setup moves + T-Perm (edges) or modified Y-Perm (corners). Each piece is solved individually. This method teaches the fundamentals of BLD piece tracing.
bld-old-pochmann.exampleFormula: T-Perm: R U R' U' R' F R2 U' R' U' R U R' F' — edge swap
drills: Practice T-Perm and Y-Perm until they're automatic with eyes closed
Trace edge cycles on a solved cube with your eyes open first

bld-memo-basics.title: BLD Memo Basics
bld-memo-basics.subtitle: Learn Speffz letter scheme and basic memorization for edges and corners
bld-memo-basics.description: Master the Speffz lettering scheme and create a basic memo system: assign letters to stickers, trace piece cycles, and create memorable words/images.
bld-memo-basics.theory: Speffz assigns one letter to each sticker (24 edge stickers = A-X, 24 corner stickers = A-X). Tracing cycles: start at buffer, follow the piece that belongs there, continue until back at buffer. Convert letter pairs into memorable images or words.
drills: Practice tracing edge cycles on a solved cube (no memo needed)
Create your letter pair image list for all 576 combinations

bld-m2-op.title: M2 for Edges
bld-m2-op.subtitle: Upgrade edge solving from Old Pochmann to M2 — faster, fewer moves per edge
bld-m2-op.description: Replace Old Pochmann edges with the M2 method: use the DF buffer and M2 move to swap pieces, with special algorithms for M-slice targets.
bld-m2-op.theory: M2 is significantly faster than OP for edges. Each edge is solved with M2 + setup moves (1-3 moves typically). M-slice targets (FU, BD, BU) require special handling. Combined with OP corners, M2/OP is the standard intermediate BLD method.
drills: Practice M2 edge execution without memo until it's fluid
Learn the special M-slice target algorithms (FU, BD, BU cases)

bld-letter-pairs.title: Letter Pair Images
bld-letter-pairs.subtitle: Build a complete letter pair image system for rapid and reliable memorization
bld-letter-pairs.description: Develop a personal letter pair image system: a unique, vivid image for every two-letter combination (AA, AB, AC... XX) for fast memo encoding.
bld-letter-pairs.theory: Letter pair images are the standard BLD memo technique. Each pair of letters becomes one mental image (e.g., QK = Quack, MB = Mobile). Images are placed in a memory palace (Roman room) or linked in a story. A good image system enables sub-30s memo.
drills: Create images for all 576 letter pairs over 2-4 weeks
Practice memo-only: memorize, wait 5 minutes, recall without solving

bld-audio-loops.title: Audio Loop Memo
bld-audio-loops.subtitle: Use rhythmic audio repetition for short-term edge memo during execution
bld-audio-loops.description: Apply audio loop memorization for edges: convert letter sequences into rhythmic sounds you repeat internally during corner execution.
bld-audio-loops.theory: Audio memo is for short-term recall (edges, executed second). Convert letter string into a rhythmic sound loop (e.g., 'KA-JE-PO-SU-TA' with rhythm). Repeating this internally during corner execution keeps it in phonological working memory. Enables sub-15s edge memo.
drills: Practice converting 6-8 letter strings into audio loops
Test: memo edges with audio, solve corners OP, recall edges from audio

bld-3-style.title: 3-Style Commutators
bld-3-style.subtitle: Solve 3 pieces per algorithm using pure commutators — the fastest BLD method
bld-3-style.description: Transition to full 3-Style: solve 3 edges or 3 corners with one commutator algorithm (8-12 moves), replacing piece-by-piece methods entirely.
bld-3-style.theory: 3-Style uses commutators of the form [A, B] = A B A' B' to cycle 3 pieces. Each cycle solves 2 pieces (buffer + 2 targets) with one algorithm. Full 3-Style requires ~800 algorithms. Most cubers learn a subset of the most common cases.
bld-3-style.exampleFormula: [R U R', D2] = R U R' D2 R U' R' D2 — corner commutator
drills: Start with 3-Style corners (easier, fewer cases) then progress to edges
Learn 5 new commutators per week until you've covered the common cases

bld-multi.title: Multi-BLD
bld-multi.subtitle: Solve multiple cubes blindfolded in one attempt — memory palace mastery
bld-multi.description: Extend BLD to multiple cubes: memorize and solve 2+ cubes blindfolded consecutively using memory palaces and long-term memo techniques.
bld-multi.theory: Multi-BLD scales BLD memo from short-term to long-term memory. Each cube gets its own memory palace location. Review system: memo cubes 1-N, then mentally review all before starting execution. World-class: 50+ cubes blindfolded.
drills: Start with 2 cubes, add 1 per successful attempt
Build and practice with 5+ memory palace locations

bld-4bld-5bld.title: BigBLD (4BLD/5BLD)
bld-4bld-5bld.subtitle: Extend BLD to 4x4 and 5x5 cubes with center, wing, and corner systems
bld-4bld-5bld.description: Apply BLD principles to 4x4 and 5x5 cubes: additional piece types (centers, wings, midges), specialized commutators, and expanded memo systems.
bld-4bld-5bld.theory: 4BLD/5BLD add centers and wing edges to the standard BLD challenge. Centers require orientation awareness. 4x4 uses U2/r2 methods as a stepping stone from M2/OP. 5x5 adds midges. The memo load scales significantly — 5BLD requires ~100+ targets.
drills: Start 4BLD with U2 centers + r2 wings + OP corners
Progress to 3-Style for all piece types as you advance

fmc-blockbuilding.title: FMC Blockbuilding
fmc-blockbuilding.subtitle: Construct efficient 2x2x2 and 2x2x3 blocks as the FMC foundation
fmc-blockbuilding.description: Learn systematic block building for FMC: start with a 2x2x2 block, expand to 2x2x3, then extend to F2L-1 — prioritizing low move counts over speed.
fmc-blockbuilding.theory: FMC block building is fundamentally different from speedsolving: you're optimizing for moves, not time. Start with the easiest 2x2x2 (look for pre-built pairs), expand to 2x2x3, then leave one F2L slot unsolved (F2L-1) to enable better last layer options.
drills: Build 2x2x2 blocks from 10 scrambles, aim for ≤6 moves each
Expand each to 2x2x3 in ≤8 additional moves

fmc-pseudo-blocks.title: Pseudo Blocks & Pre-Moves
fmc-pseudo-blocks.subtitle: Build blocks relative to offset centers using pre-moves for flexibility
fmc-pseudo-blocks.description: Use pre-moves and pseudo blocks to find shorter block solutions by temporarily ignoring center alignment.
fmc-pseudo-blocks.theory: A pre-move is applied BEFORE the scramble to shift piece positions. Pseudo blocks are solved relative to an offset center. These techniques dramatically expand the blockbuilding possibilities, often saving 2-4 moves on the 2x2x2 or 2x2x3 phase.
drills: Practice finding 2x2x2 pseudo blocks — compare move count with standard
Learn to write pre-moves and reverse them at the end of the solution

fmc-niss.title: NISS Technique
fmc-niss.subtitle: Normal-Inverse Scramble Switch: find solutions on both scramble directions
fmc-niss.description: Master NISS: solve on the inverse scramble to find opportunities invisible from the normal direction, switching back and forth for optimal solutions.
fmc-niss.theory: NISS is arguably the most powerful single technique in FMC. A sequence found on the inverse scramble, when reversed, is a valid sequence on the normal scramble. Switching lets you find continuations for both. Most sub-30 FMC solutions use NISS.
drills: Practice on a scramble: find continuations on both normal and inverse
Learn to write NISS notation: moves in parentheses are on inverse

fmc-insertions.title: Insertions (Commutator)
fmc-insertions.subtitle: Insert commutators into a skeleton for move-cancellation optimization
fmc-insertions.description: Build a skeleton (partial solution leaving 3-5 unsolved pieces), then insert commutators at optimal points to solve remaining pieces with maximum cancellation.
fmc-insertions.theory: Instead of solving the last pieces at the end, insert a commutator earlier in the solve where it cancels moves with surrounding sequences. A well-placed insertion can solve 3 corners in 8 moves but cancel 4-6, netting only 2-4 moves. This is the key to sub-28 solves.
drills: Practice building skeletons that leave exactly 3-5 corners
Use insertion finder tools to compare your insertions with optimal

fmc-edge-orientation.title: FMC Edge Orientation
fmc-edge-orientation.subtitle: Orient edges early to reduce the cube to a more manageable state
fmc-edge-orientation.description: Apply systematic edge orientation early in the FMC solution to restrict subsequent moves and simplify block building.
fmc-edge-orientation.theory: EO in FMC (similar to ZZ's first step) orients all edges so you only need R, L, U, D moves. This reduces the search space and often leads to shorter continuations. EO-first approaches are the foundation of modern DR-based FMC solving.
drills: Practice identifying misoriented edges on a given scramble
Solve EO in ≤6 moves and note how it simplifies the next steps

fmc-domino-reduction.title: Domino Reduction (DR)
fmc-domino-reduction.subtitle: Reduce the cube to a 3-color 'domino' state — the modern standard for elite FMC
fmc-domino-reduction.description: Achieve Domino Reduction: transform the cube into a state solvable using only U, D, R2, L2, F2, B2 moves — the modern standard for elite FMC solving.
fmc-domino-reduction.theory: DR is the dominant technique in modern FMC. The solve is split: (1) reach DR state (typically 10-14 moves), (2) solve from DR (typically 10-14 moves). The DR state limits available moves, making the second phase highly constrained and efficient.
drills: Practice reaching DR from random scrambles — compare move counts
Study DR solutions from top solvers (Sebastiano Tronto, Wong Chong Wen, Cale Schoon)

fmc-htr.title: Half-Turn Reduction (HTR)
fmc-htr.subtitle: Further reduce from DR to a half-turn-only state for the finish
fmc-htr.description: From a DR state, find an HTR — a further reduced state where only half-turns (R2, L2, U2, D2, F2, B2) are needed to solve the cube.
fmc-htr.theory: HTR is an advanced extension of DR. From DR, solve corner permutation and some edges to reach a state solvable with only half-turns. The final phase from HTR to solved is extremely constrained, often yielding very short solutions.
drills: From a DR state, practice finding HTR continuations
Learn HTR triggers and common HTR patterns

fmc-full-mastery.title: FMC Full Mastery
fmc-full-mastery.subtitle: Complete FMC proficiency: consistent sub-25 solutions with advanced techniques
fmc-full-mastery.description: Achieve complete FMC mastery capable of consistent sub-25 (and often sub-23) solutions using DR, HTR, optimized insertions, and NISS.
fmc-full-mastery.theory: Full FMC mastery combines all techniques: DR/HTR for efficient solves, NISS for expanded search, insertions for final optimization, and the ability to evaluate multiple approaches in 60 minutes. The world's best average under 23 moves in competition.
drills: Complete 25 official FMC attempts (60 min each, no tools)
Analyze each attempt: where could you have saved moves?

cube-theory-basics.title: Cube Theory Basics
cube-theory-basics.subtitle: Understand parity, permutation parity, and why certain states are impossible
cube-theory-basics.description: Learn fundamental cube theory: why a single edge flip or corner twist is impossible, the concept of parity, and how permutation parity constrains cube states.
cube-theory-basics.theory: The cube has mathematical invariants: total edge flip parity must be even, total corner twist must be a multiple of 3, and overall permutation parity must be even. Understanding these explains why certain OLL/PLL combinations occur and helps with algorithm design.
drills: Prove to yourself: can you flip exactly one edge? Twist one corner?
Calculate the number of possible cube states (43 quintillion)

commutators-theory.title: Commutator Theory
commutators-theory.subtitle: Understand [A, B] = A B A' B' structure for creating custom algorithms
commutators-theory.description: Master commutator theory: design your own algorithms using the commutator/conjugate framework. Essential for BLD, FMC, and advanced method development.
commutators-theory.theory: A commutator [A, B] cycles pieces where A and B's affected areas overlap. Pure commutators affect only the intersection of affected pieces. Conjugates (setup + alg + undo setup) extend this to any position. This is the core concept behind 3-Style BLD and FMC insertions.
commutators-theory.exampleFormula: [R U R', D2] — the commutator swaps 3 corners
drills: Write 10 different commutators and trace which pieces they affect
Design a commutator that cycles 3 specific edges of your choice

group-theory-cube.title: Group Theory & The Cube
group-theory-cube.subtitle: Apply mathematical group theory to understand cube structure and solve optimization
group-theory-cube.description: Study the cube as a mathematical group: generators, subgroups, cosets, and how God's Number (20) was proven using group theory and computer search.
group-theory-cube.theory: The Rubik's cube group has order ~4.3×10^19. Key subgroups: the square group (only half-turns), the 2-gen group (RU). Understanding group structure enables optimal solving. Kociemba's two-phase algorithm exploits the subgroup chain: cube → H-group → solved.
drills: Study the cube group's generators and how they relate to solving methods
Explore the square group by solving with only half-turns

optimal-solving-theory.title: Optimal Solving Theory
optimal-solving-theory.subtitle: Understand Kociemba's two-phase algorithm and how computers find optimal solutions
optimal-solving-theory.description: Study how optimal solvers work: phase-based reduction, pruning tables, IDA* search, and why finding truly optimal solutions is computationally feasible.
optimal-solving-theory.theory: Kociemba's algorithm reduces the cube in two phases: (1) to the H-group, (2) from H-group to solved. Pruning tables prune the search tree. This finds solutions ≤20 moves in milliseconds, enabling real-time analysis and scramble verification.
drills: Use a cube solver to analyze the optimal solution for your solves
Compare your cross solution to the optimal cross from a solver

algorithm-optimization.title: Algorithm Optimization
algorithm-optimization.subtitle: Analyze, compare, and select optimal algs based on speed, ergonomics, and context
algorithm-optimization.description: Develop the skill to evaluate algorithms critically: compare alternatives, measure execution speed, assess regrip cost, and select the best option for YOUR hands.
algorithm-optimization.theory: An algorithm isn't just about move count — it's about finger trick compatibility, regrip count, transition smoothness from the previous step, and personal ergonomics. Top cubers often know 2-3 alternatives per case and choose based on hand position.
drills: For each PLL, try all 3-4 common algs and pick the fastest for you
Audit your algorithm set: replace any alg with ≥1s execution time

method-comparison.title: Method Comparison & Selection
method-comparison.subtitle: Understand trade-offs between CFOP, Roux, ZZ, and Petrus for different goals
method-comparison.description: Analyze the strengths and weaknesses of major methods: CFOP (algorithmic, high TPS), Roux (intuitive, low moves), ZZ (rotationless, oriented), Petrus (block building).
method-comparison.theory: CFOP: highest TPS potential, largest community, most resources. Roux: lowest average move count (~48), intuitive, M-slice heavy. ZZ: rotationless, guaranteed edge orientation, natural ZBLL pairing. Petrus: excellent for FMC, builds spatial awareness.
drills: Complete 25 solves with each method and compare your splits
Identify which method's strengths align with your natural abilities

elite-theory.title: Elite Theory & Innovation
elite-theory.subtitle: Contribute to cubing knowledge: discover new algs, optimize methods, or develop novel techniques
elite-theory.description: Reach the frontier of cubing theory where you can generate novel algorithms, propose method improvements, or contribute new techniques to the community.
elite-theory.theory: The cutting edge of cubing theory involves algorithm generation (using computer search with CubeExplorer or ksolve), method hybridization (combining concepts from different methods), and technique innovation. This is where the next generation of world records comes from.
drills: Use CubeExplorer or ksolve to generate optimized algs for a specific case
Propose and test a method hybridization idea over 100 solves
